points: The Appellate Tribunal makes a final decision on an appeal or proceedings.
This final decision must be delivered as a Judgment.
88.example: A company named Meera Textiles Private Limited has a legal case running before the Appellate Tribunal. After reviewing the arguments, the Tribunal is ready to conclude the case. According to the rules, the Tribunal officially delivers its final decision by issuing a Judgment.

terms.meaning: A higher body that reviews decisions made by lower authorities.
The official final decision given by a court or tribunal.

88.watch: Do not confuse this rule with rules about how an appeal is filed, as this only covers how the final decision is delivered.

89.summary: This rule explains how the final decisions of a Tribunal bench must be written down. It ensures that the core ruling is easy to find. Every order or direction must appear clearly in the final paragraph.
points: All decisions must be in clear and precise terms.
The final paragraph must contain the operative portion.
This rule applies to orders and directions of the Bench.
89.example: Meera Textiles Private Limited filed an appeal before the Tribunal bench. After hearing all the arguments, the bench decided the case. To follow the rules, the judges made sure that their final decision and all directions were written down in clear and precise terms in the very last paragraph of the order document.

terms.meaning: A panel of judges or legal officers hearing a case.
The main part of an order that states what must actually be done.

89.watch: Do not look for the final decision in the middle of the document, as the rule requires it to be at the very end.

90.summary: This rule explains how corrections are handled in official orders. The specific Member of the Bench who writes the order must sign off on any changes. They do this by putting their initials on the corrections and at the bottom of every page.
points: The order must be prepared by a Member of the Bench.
That same Member must initial all corrections made in the text.
The Member must also place their initials at the bottom of each page.
90.example: Meera Textiles Private Limited is involved in a legal dispute. After the hearing, a Bench Member named Justice Rao prepares the final order. While reviewing the document, Justice Rao notices a small typo in the company name and corrects it. Following the rules, Justice Rao initials right next to the corrected typo and also puts his initials at the bottom of every single page of the order.

terms.meaning: An official judge or officer who sits on the tribunal to hear and decide cases.
To write the first letters of one's name as a quick signature.

90.watch: People often think any office staff can fix mistakes in an order, but only the specific Member who prepared it can make and initial the corrections.

91.summary: This rule explains how the Appellate Tribunal announces its decisions. It says the decision should normally be read right after the hearing ends, or notified in a cause list if it is delayed. Reading just the main working part of the order in an open court is considered the official announcement.
points: The tribunal tries to announce the order immediately after the hearing ends.
If orders are kept pending for later, the announcement date is put in the cause list.
The cause list notice serves as a valid intimation of the order being announced.
Reading only the operative portion in open court counts as the official pronouncement.
91.example: In a dispute involving Meera Textiles Private Limited, the hearing at the Appellate Tribunal ended today. Instead of announcing the decision immediately, the judges kept the order reserved. A few days later, the date for the announcement was officially published in the cause list. On that scheduled day, the tribunal read out only the operative portion of the order in the open court, which completed the official announcement process as required by the rules.

terms.meaning: A higher forum that reviews decisions.
An official schedule or list of cases to be heard or announced.
The main working part of the decision that states what needs to be done.

91.watch: People often think the entire order must be read aloud, but reading just the main working part in open court is enough.

92.summary: This rule allows any single member of the Appellate Tribunal to announce a final decision for the whole Bench. When this happens, a staff member called the Court Master must write a note in the official file. This note states that the decision was read out in open court on behalf of the entire Bench.
points: Any one member can read out the order for the whole Bench.
The Court Master must record this event in the order sheet.
The note must confirm that the order was pronounced in open court.
92.example: Meera Textiles Private Limited had a pending case at the Appellate Tribunal. On the day of the final decision, only one Member of the Bench was present in the courtroom. That single Member read out the order on behalf of the whole Bench. Immediately after, the Court Master wrote a note in the official order sheet confirming that the Bench's order was announced in open court.

terms.meaning: A higher official body that hears appeals against lower decisions.
To officially and formally announce a decision out loud.
An official helper in the court who manages records and notes.

92.watch: Do not assume that every member of the Bench needs to be present to read out the final order.

93.summary: This rule explains what happens when the judges who heard a case are gone or unavailable to read out the final decision. The Chairperson can ask another judge to read out the decision if it was already prepared and signed. However, if a judge cannot sign the order because of death, retirement, resignation, or another reason, the case must be heard all over again.
points: The Chairperson can authorize any Member to pronounce an order if the original Bench members are unavailable or left.
The authorized Member must check that the order was already prepared and signed by the original Bench.
The authorized Member must sign the order sheet and state that they pronounced the order.
If an order cannot be signed due to death, retirement, resignation, or any other reason, the case is treated as part-heard and listed for a fresh hearing.
93.example: At the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal, a bench of two Members heard a dispute involving Meera Textiles Private Limited and finished writing their order. Before they could read it out, both Members retired. The Chairperson checked the ready order, verified their signatures, and authorized another Member, Mr. Sharma, to pronounce it. Mr. Sharma read the order in court and signed the order sheet to record that he did so on behalf of the original Bench.

terms.meaning: A panel of judges or members hearing a case.
A higher body that hears appeals against lower orders or decisions.
To officially announce or read out a decision in public.

93.watch: Do not confuse simply reading out a signed order with a fresh hearing, which only happens if the original members could not even sign it.

94.summary: This rule explains what the Court Master must do right after the Appellate Tribunal announces an order. The Court Master must write important details on the case file and record them in the court diary. These details include the date, how the case was disposed of, and which members made up the Bench.
points: The Court Master must act immediately when an order is pronounced.
An endorsement must be made on the case file with specific details.
Entries must be updated in the official court diary.
94.example: In a dispute involving Alpha Logistics Private Limited and Beta Transports Private Limited, the Appellate Tribunal finally announces its order. Straight away, the Court Master takes the case file and writes down the date of the decision, how the matter was disposed of, and the names of the judges on the Bench. Finally, the Court Master records these exact details in the court diary.

terms.meaning: A higher body that hears appeals against orders.
An official who manages court records and assists during hearings.
The final conclusion or settlement of a case.

94.watch: Do not confuse this with the judges writing the order, as this rule only applies to the Court Master recording the details after the order is announced.

95.summary: This rule explains how an official order moves inside the tribunal after it is pronounced. First, the Court Master sends the order and case file to the Deputy Registrar. Next, the Deputy Registrar checks that all rules were followed and signs the file, before sending it to the Registry to make and send copies to the parties.
points: The Court Master sends the order and case file to the Deputy Registrar right after pronouncing the order.
The Deputy Registrar checks the file to ensure the rules were followed and initials it with the date.
The Deputy Registrar then sends the case file and order to the Registry for making and sharing copies with the parties.
95.example: After a hearing involving Alpha Beta Private Limited, the Court Master immediately hands the order and case file to the Deputy Registrar. The Deputy Registrar carefully reviews the file to ensure every rule was followed, then marks their initials and the date on the cover. Finally, the Deputy Registrar sends the file to the Registry so that official copies can be prepared and sent to the parties involved in the case.

terms.meaning: An official who assists the judge or tribunal during court proceedings and handles case files.
An administrative officer in the tribunal who helps manage case records and checks rules.
The administrative office of the tribunal that handles paperwork, files, and sends copies to parties.

95.watch: Remember that this rule only covers the internal movement of files between tribunal staff, not what the parties must do.

96.summary: This rule explains the exact formatting requirements for orders made by the Tribunal. Every order must be neatly typed on one side of the paper with specific margins and spacing. Additionally, the Members of the Bench must sign the order in a particular order and direction.
points: Orders must be neatly typewritten in double space.
Use only one side of durable A-4 size foolscap folio paper.
Leave a 5 cm margin on the left and a 2.5 cm margin on the right.
Leave sufficient space at the top and bottom of each page.
Members of the Bench must sign from right to left based on seniority.
96.example: Meera Textiles Private Limited recently received an order from the Tribunal. When the company checked the physical document, they noticed it was typewritten in double space on durable A-4 size paper, using only one side. The left margin was 5 cm wide while the right margin was 2.5 cm wide, with neat corrections and enough blank space at the top and bottom of every page. At the end of the document, the Members of the Bench had signed their names starting from the right and moving toward the left according to their seniority.

terms.meaning: A panel of members or judges sitting together to hear cases and make decisions.
The order of status or length of service of the members.

96.watch: Do not forget that signatures must go from right to left based on seniority, not left to right.

97.summary: This rule explains what happens to a case file after the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal issues its order. The assigned official must organize the papers with page numbers and an index sheet. Finally, the official initials the records and sends them to the records room.
points: Applies after the order is communicated to the parties or their legal representatives.
The official must arrange the records and add page numbers.
An Index Sheet in a prescribed form must be prepared.
The official initials the records and sends them to the records room.
97.example: After the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal communicated its order in a dispute involving Acme Logistics Private Limited, the assigned official took charge of the paperwork. The official carefully organized all the case documents, added page numbers to every sheet, and filled out the required Index Sheet. After signing with initials to confirm the work was done, the official securely transmitted the complete file to the records room for permanent storage.

terms.meaning: The act of adding page numbers to the pages of a document or file.
To send or pass something from one place to another.

97.watch: Do not assume this rule allows parties to view the records room without following separate procedural permissions.

98.summary: This rule explains how files, records, and orders of cases must be moved. Such items can only be sent after someone signs to show they received them. This record of movement is kept in a register as instructed by the Registrar.
points: Files, records, and case orders can be transmitted only after getting an acknowledgement.
The acknowledgement must be recorded in a movement register.
Different sections or levels maintain these registers following the Registrar's directions.
98.example: At Apex Tribunal, Clerk Amit needs to send a stack of case records from the filing section to the judicial section. Before handing over the stack, Amit asks the receiving clerk to sign the movement register to confirm receipt, strictly following the Registrar's directions. Only after obtaining this acknowledgement are the files moved.

terms.meaning: The act of sending something from one place or person to another.
An official responsible for keeping official records and giving directions for office procedures.

98.watch: Do not assume you can send files informally without signing the movement register first.

99.summary: This rule explains how final orders must be stored and organized in the library by the Registry. Each month, orders are kept together by date, indexed, and stitched in a folder. At the end of every year, a yearly index is also made and kept in a separate file for lawyers to check.
points: The officer in charge sends copies of every final order to the library.
Monthly orders are kept in a separate folder, arranged by date, indexed, and stitched.
A yearly consolidated index is prepared at the end of every year and kept in a separate file.
Order folders and indices can be used by legal practitioners for reference in the library.
99.example: At ABC Textiles Private Limited, a final order is issued by the tribunal. The officer in charge of the Registry sends this order to the library. All orders received during the month are placed in a separate folder, arranged by the date they were announced, and neatly indexed and stitched together. When December ends, the staff makes a consolidated yearly index and keeps it in a separate file. Later, when an advocate visits the library, these organized folders and indices are made available for them to view and read as reference.

terms.meaning: The administrative office of the tribunal.
The formal announcement of an order.
Lawyers or advocates.

99.watch: People often confuse monthly folders with yearly files, but monthly orders are stitched and kept in folders while the yearly index is kept in a separate file.

100.summary: This rule requires the Judicial Branch to keep a special book called a register for appeals and special leave petitions sent to the Supreme Court. The head of the tribunal, called the Chairperson, must check this register during the first week of every month. This helps keep track of cases moving from the Appellate Tribunal to the highest court.
points: A register in Form NCLAT-9 must be maintained for Special Leave Petitions and Appeals to the Supreme Court.
The Judicial Branch is responsible for making prompt entries in this register.
The Chairperson must scrutinize the register in the first week of every month.
100.example: At Zenith Infra Private Limited, a recent order was challenged by filing an appeal to the Supreme Court against a decision of the Appellate Tribunal. The Judicial Branch immediately recorded this case details in a special book named Form NCLAT-9. In the first week of the next month, the Chairperson reviewed this register to ensure all Supreme Court appeals were properly entered and up to date.

terms.meaning: A request made to the Supreme Court to allow an appeal against an order.
The head officer in charge of the tribunal.
The office department responsible for handling legal records and court cases.

100.watch: Do not assume this rule applies to all company cases, as it only covers appeals and petitions going to the Supreme Court.

101.summary: This rule explains what happens when the Supreme Court of India passes an order regarding a case from the Appellate Tribunal. The order must be shown to the leaders of the Tribunal right away and put in the case file. Also, the Registrar must be told immediately if the Supreme Court gave any directions that need to be followed.
points: Supreme Court orders are placed before the Chairperson or Members for information.
The order is kept safely in the relevant case file.
The Registrar's immediate attention is drawn to any directions that require compliance.
101.example: The Supreme Court of India passed a final order in a legal dispute involving Sunshine Logistics Private Limited and an earlier decision by the Appellate Tribunal. As soon as the official order reached the Tribunal, staff members brought it straight to the Chairperson to read. They placed the paper inside the official case file for Sunshine Logistics Private Limited. Because the Supreme Court gave specific directions in the text that the Tribunal needed to follow, the staff immediately notified the Registrar to take action.

terms.meaning: A temporary or a final decision made by a court.
A higher body that reviews decisions made by lower authorities.
An official responsible for keeping records and managing administrative tasks.

101.watch: People often confuse this rule as a way to file a new appeal, but it is only about handling orders that have already been passed by the Supreme Court.

102.summary: The given rule states that the Registrar must quickly follow the orders given by the Supreme Court. It falls under the miscellaneous provisions of the regulations. The text is very brief and does not provide extra details.
points: The Registrar must take quick action.
The Registrar must follow Supreme Court directions.
102.example: In a legal dispute involving Apex Builders Private Limited, the Supreme Court issued a specific order regarding company records. Based on the rule, the Registrar must take quick steps to follow these directions without any unnecessary delay.

terms.meaning: An official who handles company records and administration.
Done with speed and efficiency.

102.watch: Do not assume any specific deadlines or time limits because the text does not mention them.

103.summary: The Appellate Tribunal can allow people to file appeals and other proceedings online using electronic media. It can also let people fix errors in their filings using email or the internet. The Central Government may give instructions about this from time to time.
points: The Appellate Tribunal may permit online filing of appeals and proceedings.
Errors in electronic filings can be fixed through email or the internet.
The Central Government can issue instructions from time to time regarding these electronic filings.
103.example: Aarav wanted to submit an appeal for his company, Sharma Enterprises Private Limited, to the Appellate Tribunal. Instead of taking physical papers to the office, the Tribunal allowed him to use the online filing system. Later, Aarav received an email stating there was a mistake in his documents. Following the new electronic rules, he was able to fix the defect quickly through the internet as permitted by the Tribunal.

terms.meaning: A higher official body that reviews decisions made by lower authorities.
The act of fixing a mistake or defect.

103.watch: Do not assume online filing is available immediately, as a specific date must be notified separately.

104.summary: This rule gives the Chairperson of the Appellate Tribunal the power to handle situations not covered by the existing rules. If the rules are silent or lack a provision, the Chairperson can issue directions, orders, or circulars. This helps solve difficulties that come up during the working of the Tribunal.
points: The Chairperson can act when the rules are silent.
Appropriate directions may be issued to remove difficulties.
Orders or circulars can be created to govern new situations.
104.example: A new procedural issue arises during a case at Meera Textiles Private Limited before the Appellate Tribunal, but the existing rulebook does not explain how to handle it. Because the rules are silent on this specific matter, the Chairperson steps in to issue a special direction. This order governs the unexpected contingency so the Tribunal can continue its work smoothly without getting stuck.

terms.meaning: A higher body that reviews decisions made by lower authorities.
An unexpected event or situation that may occur.
Despite anything else stated.

104.watch: People often confuse this power as applying to all laws, but it only applies when the specific rules are silent.
